intro.why: ML systems fail differently from ordinary software: through drift, corrupted or biased data, and hidden failures on small groups. Quality has to be tested at every layer, and in production.

symbols: true positives, false positives, false negatives
harmonic mean of precision and recall
framework of LLM-judged metrics for RAG pipelines

sections.title: OOP for agents: the production-crew analogy
sections.plain: A film crew of specialists beats one director doing every job.
sections.body:
Procedural approach: one director does everything: a giant loop of if/else statements guiding the LLM. Fragile and hard to scale.

OOP crew: a base "Crew Member" (the Agent class). The Director is a ValidationAgent, the Writer a SummaryAgent, the Cinematographer a FormattingAgent (inheritance). Each works in its own bubble (encapsulation). The production workflow assembles them (composition). The producer just says "Execute!" and each does its own job (polymorphism). Adding a Sound Engineer means writing one new subclass, without touching the others.

sections.title: Traditional vs ML testing; ML test types and the pyramid
sections.plain: Test the data, the model and the infrastructure, not just the code.
sections.body:
Traditional softwareML systems
LogicExplicit, written by developersLearned from data
What tests verifyOutputs of the logicThe learning process, data integrity, statistical outputs
Why it failsBugs in codeConcept drift, data corruption, biased data (as well as bugs)
Test typeChecks
Data testsSchemas, missing values, distributions
Model testsPerformance, fairness, robustness to edge cases
Infrastructure testsStress-testing serving APIs, latency
Heuristic testsCommon-sense rules (age ≥ 0)

ML test pyramid: base: data and code unit tests (schema validation, data cleaning, feature pipelines); middle: model tests (performance, fairness, staleness, overfitting); top: system tests (end-to-end pipeline, UI, integration). Many cheap tests at the bottom, few expensive ones at the top.

sections.title: The MLOps control loop
sections.plain: Validate, train, register, deploy, monitor, retrain, around and around.
sections.body:
1. Raw data storage
  2. Data validation (on failure: alert and quarantine)
  3. Feature store
  4. Training orchestrator
  5. Model registry and CI/CD
  6. Deploy to production
  7. Monitor the system and drift
  8. Metrics and dashboards
  9. Trigger retraining → back to step 1

Quality gates sit at every arrow: bad data never reaches training, bad models never reach the registry's champion alias, and drift triggers retraining.

sections.title: Data quality and validation
sections.plain: Garbage in, garbage out: validate automatically before training.
sections.body:
Why: garbage in, garbage out; data quality is an upper bound on model performance; historical bias gets amplified; pipelines fail silently. Automated validation before training is mandatory.

DimensionMeaningExample
AccuracyReflects the real worldChurn labels are correct
CompletenessNo missing records or nullsEvery profile has age and location
ConsistencyUniform formatsDates always YYYY-MM-DD
TimelinessUp to dateStock prices delayed under 1 s
Validation pipeline
  1. Ingestion
  2. Schema check gate: missing columns, type changes
  3. Value check gate: impossible ranges, outliers
  4. Label health gate: class imbalance, missing labels
  5. Action gateway: halt if mismatched

Pydantic demo: record 1 passes; record 2 fails (age must be ≥ 0); record 3 fails (age required); the pipeline continues with the one valid record. Code example ex1 extends this with a date-format check and a halt threshold.

sections.title: Pipeline quality and CI for ML
sections.plain: The automated sequence itself must be reliable, repeatable and versioned.
sections.body:
Pipeline quality = robustness of the automated sequence: idempotency (same inputs → same outputs, safe to rerun), versioning (code, data and models linked), orchestration (Airflow, Kubeflow).

ChangeCI action
Any commitSyntax checks and unit tests
Model architecture changeTrain on a small synthetic dataset (smoke test)
Schema updateValidate against historical data
All passProduce a deployable artifact in the registry

sections.title: Model quality: metrics and slicing
sections.plain: Pick metrics that fit the problem, and check every important subgroup.
sections.body:
Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data. Model quality also covers interpretability, fairness and efficiency; always test on unseen data; quality degrades over time.

$$\text{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\quad \text{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\quad F_1=\frac{2\,PR}{P+R},\quad \text{RMSE}=\sqrt{\tfrac1n\textstyle\sum(y-\hat y)^2}$$

RMSE penalises large errors more heavily than mean absolute error.

Slicing: 95% global accuracy might be 50% on a minority group. Slice by gender, location, device…, compute per-slice metrics, then mitigate or retrain. Illustration: overall 95%: slice A/desktop 98%, B/web 94%, C/mobile about 48%: a critical failure. Demo: global 62.50%, desktop 100%, mobile 25%. In code example ex1, global accuracy is 0.949 while the mobile slice gets 0.473.

sections.title: Training vs inference testing
sections.plain: Training tests check learning; inference tests check speed and stability.
sections.body:
TrainingInference
GoalLearning capability and convergencePrediction speed, output format, stability
ComputeHigh throughput, long batch jobsLow latency, real-time, high concurrency
Failure modesExploding gradients, out of memoryAPI timeouts, incompatible input shapes
EnvironmentOffline, isolated clustersOnline, highly available servers

sections.title: System quality and telemetry
sections.plain: The model is a small part; the whole system must work and be watched.
sections.body:
The model is often less than 5% of the codebase. UI/UX, database reliability and the network matter: a perfect model behind a failing front end delivers zero value. Quality is cross-functional.

TelemetryExamples
System metricsCPU, memory, latency
Model metricsPrediction distribution, confidence, anomaly rates
Business metricsClick-through rate, conversion, revenue
AlertingThresholds that page someone

sections.title: Testing in production: A/B, shadow, canary
sections.plain: Offline tests can't show real impact; route some live traffic carefully.
sections.body:
Why experiment in production: offline data is static; real systems have feedback loops; only live traffic proves business impact. It requires traffic-routing infrastructure.

StrategyRoutingUsers see v2?
A/B teste.g. 90% v1 / 10% v2Yes, both serve users
Shadow100% v1 serves; a copy goes to v2No: v2's outputs are only logged
Canary99% v1 / 1% v2, gradually increasedA small, growing share

Code example ex2 simulates a v2 with a hidden 8% bug: A/B exposes about 2,000 users (around 180 hit), shadow exposes none, canary about 600 (around 50 hit) before it would be caught.

sections.title: Security threats across the ML lifecycle
sections.plain: Attackers can poison data, plant backdoors, compromise dependencies or fool and copy the model.
sections.body:
ML creates a new attack surface: attackers manipulate training data or inference requests; the model weights are intellectual property; training data may be private. Do threat modelling early.

StageThreat
Data collectionData poisoning (malicious records)
TrainingBackdoor attacks
DeploymentSupply-chain attacks (vulnerable or malicious libraries)
API servingEvasion / adversarial inputs; model stealing

Data collection and deployment are the most targeted stages.

sections.title: Evaluating RAG systems with RAGAS
sections.plain: Grade the retriever and the generator separately, with an LLM as judge.
sections.body:
BLEU and ROUGE (word overlap with a reference) can't detect hallucination or irrelevant context. RAGAS uses an LLM as judge, needing no human labels.

Two pipelines: offline indexing (raw documents → chunking → embedding model → vector DB) and online retrieval (user query → embedding → vector search → top-k chunks → LLM generation).

MetricComparesGrades
FaithfulnessAnswer vs retrieved context (is every claim supported?)Generator
Answer relevanceAnswer vs queryGenerator
Context precisionRetrieved context vs query (no junk)Retriever
Context recallRetrieved context vs ground truth (no missing facts)Retriever

Demo with two samples (the capital of France; what causes ocean tides) gives context recall 1.0. Code example ex2 uses simple overlap scores to show the diagnostic logic: high context recall with low faithfulness means the generator ignored good context.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Great Expectations, pandera and TFDV are common data-validation libraries; Evidently and WhyLabs monitor drift.
  • Test the tests: a validation gate that never fails may be checking nothing.
  • LLM judges can be biased (toward longer answers, their own style); calibrate them against some human labels.
  • Statistical significance: A/B tests need enough traffic and a pre-registered metric, or noise will look like improvement.

code.title: Data validation gates and slice-based evaluation
code.explain: Pydantic quarantines records with negative ages, missing fields or wrong date formats and the action gateway halts when the failure rate is too high; a classifier with 0.949 global accuracy scores 0.473 on the mobile slice.
code.notes: In production use a validation library and store quarantined rows for inspection.
code.code:
"""Data-quality gates before training, then slice-based model evaluation.

1) Pydantic validates each incoming record; invalid ones are quarantined and the
   pipeline continues only with valid data (halting if too many fail).
2) A classifier that looks fine globally is evaluated per device slice.
"""
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

class Customer(BaseModel):
    customer_id: str
    age: int = Field(..., ge=0, le=120)
    monthly_spend: float = Field(..., ge=0)
    signup_date: str = Field(..., pattern=r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$")   # consistency: YYYY-MM-DD
    churned: Optional[int] = Field(None, ge=0, le=1)

raw = [
    {"customer_id": "c1", "age": 34, "monthly_spend": 52.0, "signup_date": "2024-02-11", "churned": 0},
    {"customer_id": "c2", "age": -5, "monthly_spend": 18.0, "signup_date": "2024-03-02", "churned": 1},
    {"customer_id": "c3", "monthly_spend": 40.0, "signup_date": "2024-01-20", "churned": 0},
    {"customer_id": "c4", "age": 51, "monthly_spend": 77.5, "signup_date": "11/05/2024", "churned": 0},
    {"customer_id": "c5", "age": 29, "monthly_spend": 12.0, "signup_date": "2024-04-30", "churned": 1},
]
valid, quarantine = [], []
for r in raw:
    try:
        valid.append(Customer(**r))
    except ValidationError as e:
        quarantine.append((r["customer_id"], "; ".join(f"{x['loc'][0]}: {x['msg']}" for x in e.errors())))
print(f"schema/value gate: {len(valid)} passed, {len(quarantine)} quarantined")
for cid, why in quarantine: print(f"  {cid}: {why}")
fail_rate = len(quarantine) / len(raw)
print("action gateway:", "HALT pipeline (fail rate %.0f%% > 50%%)" % (100 * fail_rate) if fail_rate > 0.5 else "continue with valid records")
labels = [c.churned for c in valid]
print("label health: missing labels =", labels.count(None), "| class balance =", {k: labels.count(k) for k in set(labels)})

# ---- slicing ---------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
device = rng.choice(["desktop", "web", "mobile"], size=n, p=[0.55, 0.38, 0.07])
X = rng.normal(size=(n, 3)); y = (X[:, 0] + 0.5 * X[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
# on mobile the relationship is different (e.g. a UI change altered behaviour)
mob = device == "mobile"; y[mob] = (X[mob, 2] > 0).astype(int)
tr = rng.random(n) < 0.6
model = LogisticRegression().fit(X[tr], y[tr]); p = model.predict(X[~tr])
yt, dt = y[~tr], device[~tr]
print(f"\nglobal: acc {accuracy_score(yt, p):.3f}  precision {precision_score(yt, p):.3f}  recall {recall_score(yt, p):.3f}  F1 {f1_score(yt, p):.3f}")
for d in ["desktop", "web", "mobile"]:
    m = dt == d; a = accuracy_score(yt[m], p[m])
    print(f"  slice {d:<8} n={m.sum():4d}  accuracy {a:.3f}{'  <- critical failure' if a < 0.7 else ''}")

schema/value gate: 2 passed, 3 quarantined
  c2: age: Input should be greater than or equal to 0
  c3: age: Field required
  c4: signup_date: String should match pattern '^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$'
action gateway: HALT pipeline (fail rate 60% > 50%)
label health: missing labels = 0 | class balance = {0: 1, 1: 1}

global: acc 0.949  precision 0.940  recall 0.962  F1 0.951
  slice desktop  n= 908  accuracy 0.985
  slice web      n= 603  accuracy 0.983
  slice mobile   n= 112  accuracy 0.473  <- critical failure

code.title: Traffic routing strategies and RAG metric logic
code.explain: Counts users exposed to a buggy v2 under A/B, shadow and canary routing; then computes overlap-based stand-ins for faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision and context recall on two RAG samples.
mistakes: Judging RAG only by answer-reference overlap.
code.notes: Real RAGAS: evaluate(dataset, metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall]) with an LLM judge.
code.code:
"""Production experimentation and RAG evaluation.

1) Route 20,000 requests under A/B, shadow and canary strategies and count how many
   users are exposed to the new model (v2), which has a hidden bug on 8% of inputs.
2) Score two RAG answers with simple overlap-based stand-ins for the four RAGAS metrics
   (real RAGAS uses an LLM as judge; the logic of what each metric compares is the same).
"""
import random, re
random.seed(1)
N = 20_000
def v2_fails(): return random.random() < 0.08

def route(strategy):
    exposed = harmed = logged = 0
    for i in range(N):
        if strategy == "A/B":            serve_v2 = random.random() < 0.10
        elif strategy == "shadow":       serve_v2 = False; logged += 1; v2_fails()   # v2 runs silently on a copy
        elif strategy == "canary":       serve_v2 = random.random() < (0.01 if i < N // 2 else 0.05)
        if serve_v2:
            exposed += 1; harmed += v2_fails()
    return exposed, harmed, logged

for s in ["A/B", "shadow", "canary"]:
    e, h, l = route(s)
    print(f"{s:<7} users served by v2: {e:5d}  users hit by the bug: {h:4d}" + (f"  (v2 evaluated silently on {l} copies)" if l else ""))

def toks(s): return set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", s.lower())) - {"the", "a", "of", "is", "and", "by", "in", "to", "what", "how", "are"}
def overlap(a, b): A, B = toks(a), toks(b); return len(A & B) / max(1, len(A))

samples = [
    dict(q="What is the capital of France?",
         contexts=["Paris is the capital and largest city of France.", "France borders Spain and Italy."],
         answer="The capital of France is Paris.", truth="Paris is the capital of France."),
    dict(q="What causes ocean tides?",
         contexts=["Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, and also the Sun.", "Ocean salinity varies by region."],
         answer="Tides are caused by wind blowing across the ocean.", truth="The gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun causes tides."),
]
print(f"\n{'question':<32} faithful  ans_rel  ctx_prec  ctx_recall")
for s in samples:
    ctx = " ".join(s["contexts"])
    faith = overlap(s["answer"], ctx)                                   # answer claims supported by context
    ans_rel = overlap(s["q"], s["answer"])                              # answer addresses the question
    ctx_prec = sum(overlap(c, s["truth"]) > 0.3 for c in s["contexts"]) / len(s["contexts"])   # no junk retrieved
    ctx_rec = overlap(s["truth"], ctx)                                  # facts needed are present
    print(f"{s['q']:<32} {faith:8.2f} {ans_rel:8.2f} {ctx_prec:9.2f} {ctx_rec:10.2f}")
print("tides: context recall is high but faithfulness is low -> the generator ignored good context (hallucination)")

shadow  users served by v2:     0  users hit by the bug:    0  (v2 evaluated silently on 20000 copies)

question                         faithful  ans_rel  ctx_prec  ctx_recall
What is the capital of France?       1.00     1.00      0.50       1.00
What causes ocean tides?             0.50     0.67      0.50       0.83
